explanation: The action was completed earlier, so use the simple past "ate."
correct_examples: I ate dinner at seven.
She ate lunch before class.

my_sentence: I find my hair was too long, so I need to cut it.
correction: I found that my hair was too long, so I needed to cut it.
explanation: Use past tense for both the discovery and the resulting need because the story is about a completed haircut.
correct_examples: I found that my hair was too long, so I got it cut.
She realized she needed a haircut.
context: Explaining why he had a haircut.

my_sentence: Eating too much sugar will raise your blood level.
correction: Eating too much sugar will raise your blood-sugar level.
explanation: Use the compound noun "blood-sugar level" for the measurement affected by sugar intake.
correct_examples: Too much sugar can raise your blood-sugar level.
Exercise may lower blood-sugar levels.

my_sentence: If the sunset, it gets dark.
correction: If the sun sets, it gets dark.
explanation: The subject is "the sun," and the verb needs the third-person singular form "sets."
correct_examples: When the sun sets, it gets dark.
If the sun sets early, we go home.

my_sentence: If we leave for home early, we will catch the flight on time.
correction: If we leave home early, we will catch the flight on time.
explanation: The natural phrase is "leave home" when home is the starting point; no extra preposition is needed.
correct_examples: If we leave home early, we will arrive on time.
They left home at six.

my_sentence: If I had worked hard, I would had earned enough money.
correction: If I had worked hard, I would have earned enough money.
explanation: The conditional perfect is "would have + past participle"; use "have," not "had," after "would."
correct_examples: If I had worked harder, I would have earned more.
She would have passed if she had studied.

my_sentence: I haven't resigned and traveled around the world.
correction: I haven't resigned or traveled around the world.
explanation: In a negative present-perfect list, use "or" to connect the two actions that have not happened.
correct_examples: I haven't visited Japan or Korea.
She hasn't called or emailed me.
context: Explaining the unreal result of a past condition.

my_sentence: If he didn't attend college, he would not be able to find a job in big companies.
correction: If he hadn't attended college, he would not have been able to find a job in big companies.
explanation: This refers to an unreal past fact and result, so use past perfect in both parts of the third conditional.
correct_examples: If he had not attended college, he would not have found that job.
She would not have succeeded if she had quit school.

my_sentence: If he forgot to bring his kids, he would stay outside all day long.
correction: If he forgot to bring his keys, he would stay outside all day long.
explanation: The corrected sentence uses "keys" because forgetting keys causes someone to stay outside; "kids" changes the meaning.
correct_examples: If I forget my keys, I cannot get inside.
He stayed outside because he forgot his keys.

my_sentence: Can you borrow me some money for an espresso?
correction: Can you lend me some money for an espresso?
explanation: The person who gives something uses "lend"; the person who receives it uses "borrow."
correct_examples: Could you lend me some money?
I borrowed some money from my friend.
